title: The Evolution of Collective Organization and Multi-Agent Superorganisms: From Eusocial Insect Castes, Termite Cathedral Mounds, and Scale-Free Vertebrate Flocks to the 8.1-Billion-Human Planetary Superorganism
plain_title: How living things team up into giant group minds
thesis: Groups of organisms, from bacterial films and ant colonies to bird flocks and human civilization, beat the limits of a single brain by coordinating many brains, and humans did it by stacking layers of organization on top of ever-larger outside memory such as writing and computers.
summary: The paper traces 22 collective organization milestones across 3.48 billion years (within Earth's 68-moment, 4.10-billion-year census), comparing group size, total neurons, communication channels, memory and computing rates. It shows how sterile insect castes and stigmergic trails build superorganisms whose combined neurons exceed many mammal brains, how vertebrate flocks and schools maintain scale-free cohesion by tracking roughly seven neighbours, and how human polities scaled to 8.1 billion people across 10 to 11 coordination tiers sustained by an approximately 127-fold expansion in external memory for every tenfold rise in population.

claims.claim: Across human societal stages, stored outside memory scales as the 2.10 power of polity population — roughly 127 times more external storage for every tenfold growth in group size.
claims.paper_value: log10(outside memory) = −1.38 + (2.10 ± 0.28) × log10(population), R² = 0.901 (~127-fold external memory per tenfold population), contrasted with slope 0.920 ± 0.039 (R² = 0.990) when biological synaptic and genetic memory are pooled with outside storage
claims.data_value: OLS fit across the human outside-memory stages gives slope 2.10 ± 0.28, intercept −1.38, R² = 0.901 (10^2.10 = 126.9); pooling biological plus outside memory in collective_organization_evolution.csv gives slope 0.920 ± 0.039, R² = 0.990
claims.source: outside_memory_by_moment.csv and collective_organization_evolution.csv human polity rows
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: the manuscript and Figure 3B now report the exact ordinary-least-squares fit and explicitly separate external cultural storage from biological brain memory.

claims.claim: A mature leafcutter ant colony holds two trillion neurons — about 23 human brains, 314 macaque brains, or 2,630 domestic cat brains.
claims.paper_value: 2.00×10¹² collective neurons (8.0×10⁶ workers × 2.5×10⁵ neurons), equal to 23.3 human brains, 314 macaque brains, or 2,630 cat brains, running at 2.00×10¹⁵ synaptic operations per second
claims.data_value: 8.0×10⁶ × 2.5×10⁵ = 2.00×10¹² neurons and 2.00×10¹⁵ operations per second in collective_organization_evolution.csv; dividing by 8.60×10¹⁰ (human), 6.37×10⁹ (macaque) and 7.60×10⁸ (cat in cns_structural_evolution.csv) gives 23.3, 314 and 2,632
claims.source: collective_organization_evolution.csv (leafcutter row) and cns_structural_evolution.csv (human, macaque, cat rows)
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: the thousandfold unit error in the mammal-brain comparisons and the tenfold Table 1 compute offset have been corrected.

claims.claim: A cathedral termite mound holds 500 billion neurons (5.8 human brains or 78.5 macaque brains) and a honeybee hive holds 48 billion neurons (56 percent of a human brain or 75.5 marmoset brains).
claims.paper_value: termites: 5.00×10¹¹ neurons (5.8 human, 78.5 macaque) and 5.00×10¹⁴ operations per second; honeybees: 4.80×10¹⁰ neurons (0.56 human, 75.5 marmoset) and 4.80×10¹³ operations per second; Argentine ant supercolony: 7.50×10¹³ to 2.50×10¹⁴ neurons (872 to 2,910 human brains)
claims.data_value: 5.00×10¹¹ neurons and 5.00×10¹⁴ operations per second for termites; 4.80×10¹⁰ neurons and 4.80×10¹³ operations per second for honeybees in collective_organization_evolution.csv; ratios match cns_structural_evolution.csv
claims.note: Every insect colony row in Table 1 now matches both the collective ledger's neuron products and its synaptic operation rates.

claims.claim: Vertebrate schools, flocks and migratory herds aggregate tens of trillions to quadrillions of neurons without a central leader.
claims.paper_value: starling murmuration (100,000 birds): 1.90×10¹³ neurons; Atlantic herring school (10⁸ fish): 1.00×10¹⁴ neurons; Serengeti wildebeest herd (1.5×10⁶ animals): 3.75×10¹⁵ neurons
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: prose and Figure 2A neuron totals now match every swarm row in the data file.

claims.claim: Today's planetary collective combines 8.1 billion human brains (6.97×10²⁰ neurons), 15 zettabytes of outside storage (1.20×10²³ bits) and 1.89×10²² executed silicon operations per second.
claims.paper_value: 6.97×10²⁰ human neurons; 1.20×10²³ bits installed digital storage (within 1.21×10²³ total human+exosomatic collective memory); 1.89×10²² executed chip operations per second alongside 1.215×10²⁴ human synaptic operations per second (and 7.16×10²² in the CSV's 100-ops/neuron convention)
claims.data_value: 6.97×10²⁰ neurons, 1.21×10²³ collective memory bits and 7.16×10²² operations per second in collective_organization_evolution.csv; 1.20×10²³ outside bits and 1.89×10²² digital operations per second in planetary_intelligence_timeseries.csv
claims.note: Table 2 now reports the exact CSV column values while noting the 100-spike/s CSV convention versus Paper 0's 1,743-synapse/s convention.

claims.claim: With a base Dunbar band of 150 and a branching factor of 7, reaching 8.1 billion people requires 10 to 11 nested coordination levels.
claims.paper_value: N_max(L) = 150 × 7^(L − 1), giving 150 at L = 1, 1.24×10⁸ at L = 8, 6.05×10⁹ at L = 10, and 4.24×10¹⁰ at L = 11 (effective L = 10.15 for 8.1 billion people)
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: extending hierarchical depth from L = 8 to L = 10–11 makes the branching law close cleanly at planetary scale.

claims.claim: Dunbar's neocortex ratio equation predicts cohesive human face-to-face groups of about 148 individuals.
claims.paper_value: log10(N) = 0.093 + 3.389 × log10(neocortex volume ÷ rest-of-brain volume), giving 147.8 ≈ 150 at the human ratio of 4.1
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: the inverted coefficients were replaced with Dunbar's published equation, which evaluates to 147.8.

claims.claim: A cathedral termite mound plus its symbiotic fungus garden consumes about 1,000 litres of oxygen a day (~233 W total heat), while the two million termites themselves use ~15 to 40 W (25 W in the ledger).
claims.paper_value: 233 W whole-mound respiration (termites plus Termitomyces fungus comb at ~1,000 L O₂ per day), of which the insect caste biomass accounts for ~15 to 40 W (25.0 W ledger value)
claims.data_value: 25.0 W collective insect power in collective_organization_evolution.csv; 1,000 L O₂ ÷ 86,400 s × 20.1 J per mL = 232.6 W total mound+fungus respiration
claims.source: collective_organization_evolution.csv; Lüscher 1961 and Darlington et al. 1997
claims.note: Separating fungal-comb respiration (~200 W) from insect metabolism (25 W) reconciles the gas-exchange literature with the ledger.

claims.claim: Unchecked oral relays lose 73.8 percent of message fidelity across six serial hops at 20 percent error per hop, whereas 150 people already generate 11,175 social dyads.
claims.data_value: not in the project data; arithmetic reproduces exactly
claims.note: The combinatorics are exact and the per-hop error rate is explicitly presented as an illustrative communication-channel bound.

claims.claim: Starlings in a murmuration track roughly six to seven topological neighbours regardless of flock density.
claims.data_value: not in the project data; schematic trade-off curve in Figure 2B illustrates the empirical Ballerini et al. 2008 result
claims.source: Ballerini et al. 2008, PNAS 105: 1232–1237; Cavagna et al. 2010
claims.note: The seven-neighbour rule comes from 3D stereometric field reconstructions in the cited literature; Figure 2B is labelled as an illustrative cost-benefit schematic.

rationale.step: Individual brains pay ~2.3×10⁻¹⁰ watts per mammalian neuron plus pelvic and wiring penalties, so scaling cognition beyond single skulls requires multi-agent coordination.
rationale.note: Per-neuron mammalian cost (20 W ÷ 8.6×10¹⁰ = 2.3×10⁻¹⁰ W) now agrees across the text and companion papers.

rationale.step: Eusocial insects achieved superorganism integration via sterile castes and chemical stigmergy, assembling colony neuron budgets up to 23 times a human brain.
rationale.note: All colony neuron sums, synaptic rates and mammal-brain ratios now match the project's collective and CNS data files.

rationale.step: Vertebrate schools and flocks achieve rapid consensus without leaders via local topological coupling (~7 neighbours), propagating directional waves across up to 10⁸ individuals.
rationale.note: The empirical topological mechanism is solidly cited from field physics and the swarm neuron totals match the ledger.

rationale.step: Human societies scaled from bands of 150 to 8.1 billion across 10 to 11 nested hierarchy tiers, stabilised by external memory growing as the 2.10 power of group size.
rationale.note: With Dunbar's equation corrected, hierarchy depth extended to L = 10–11, and external memory regressed directly against polity size (slope 2.10, R² = 0.901), every mathematical step closes.

conclusions.conclusion: Eusocial insect colonies evolved superorganism status independently in termites and hymenopterans, reaching collective neuron counts from 0.56 to 23 human brains in single colonies (and >870 in supercolonies).
conclusions.note: Both evolutionary origins and exact neuron ratios are verified against the catalog and literature.

conclusions.conclusion: Egalitarian vertebrate swarms coordinate trillions to quadrillions of neurons over hundreds of metres through scale-free nearest-neighbour rules rather than central command.
conclusions.note: Supported by cited 3D field tracking and exact swarm row totals in collective_organization_evolution.csv.

conclusions.conclusion: Every tenfold expansion in human polity scale required roughly a 127-fold (population^2.10) expansion in durable external memory.
conclusions.note: Directly reproduced by ordinary least squares on the project's outside-memory stages (R² = 0.901).

conclusions.conclusion: Today's 8.1 billion humans and global silicon infrastructure form a planetary-scale collective holding 6.97×10²⁰ neurons and 1.20×10²³ bits of external storage.
conclusions.note: Every 2026 component agrees between Paper 5, Paper 0 and the canonical CSV ledgers.

bottom_line: Following the 24 November 2026 revision, all 22 collective milestones across 3.48 billion years, insect-to-mammal brain ratios, swarm neuron totals, Dunbar's equation (147.8), 10-to-11-tier hierarchy scaling, mound energetics (233 W total versus 25 W insects), and the population^2.10 outside-memory scaling law (~127-fold per tenfold population, R² = 0.901) reproduce cleanly from the project's data files.
revised: On 24 November 2026, Dunbar's 1992 coefficients, hierarchical branching depth (L = 10–11), the outside-memory regression (slope 2.10 ± 0.28, R² = 0.901), Table 1 and Table 2 compute and memory columns, insect colony mammal-brain ratios, vertebrate swarm neuron counts, emergence dates, mammalian per-neuron power (2.3×10⁻¹⁰ W), termite mound respiration (233 W whole-mound vs 25 W insects), and all three figures were synchronized with collective_organization_evolution.csv and outside_memory_by_moment.csv.
